blocks.text: These examples make plain what we had undertaken to prove: that certain animals are called sons and daughters without regard to age, for they are so called at any age. And the term son or daughter is then taken otherwise than in common use. For the griffin is not called son of strength because it was born of strength, but because it is strong in strength; as ἡ γὺψ [hē gyps] is strong in flight, whence it is called daughter of the wing; and the duck son of the water, because it delights in waters; and the thos son of avvi, or of barking, because it is an animal much given to barking. For the same reason [col. 231] the ostrich is called בת יענה, daughter of jaana, or of crying, not from [II, 829] age but from its cry, because it is a noisy animal ^{(7)}. But as the griffin is called not only בר גזא, son of geza, but also, by abbreviation, גזא geza or גז gez, so the ostrich is sometimes called יענה jaana for בת יענה, daughter of jaana; whence the plural יענים jeenim, Thren. IV, 3. Now, if you ask why it is called daughter and not son, whether this pertains to sex, and to what purpose God in the Law forbade the eating of the female rather than the male ostrich, the answer will not be so obvious. For the term son also applies to the female, as was evident in the trifles the Talmudists tell about the egg of the בר יוכני bar jucne, or son of jucne. But the male in a bird or quadruped is never called female. Nor will you see the word daughter embrace a whole species, except in the vulture alone, which the Chaldeans call בת כנפא, daughter of the wing, for a definite reason: namely, because they tell the fable that in that kind there are no males. Hence also in Greek, in Horapollo, ἡ γὺψ [hē gyps] is used in the feminine gender, as we shall show more fully in the chapter On רחם racham. But no one has written anything similar about the ostrich, except a few Hebrews of more recent times. Yet what I am about to say is certain: of the many names of the ostrich accepted among the Arabs, two are most in use, namely ظليم [ẓalīm] dtalim and نعام [naʿām] naam, of which the former properly denotes the male, the latter the female. But the feminine نعام [naʿām] naam is far more accepted, and in the books of the historians and geographers scarcely any other occurs. Hence the Syrians and Chaldeans call the ostrich not טלים talim but נעמא naama. In that kind, namely, the female is preferred to the male because of the eggs, which are of great value and are sought not only for eating but also for use, since vessels, and excellent ones, are made from them, as we have already [II, 830] shown above. Moreover, adult males rarely fall into human hands, because they are extremely swift. But the females are caught more often and more easily, whether they are heavy with eggs or brooding over their chicks. And their nests are visible from afar, because they are built in open places with much sand heaped up. Accordingly, as the female is better known, so her name too is far more common, and almost the only one in the mouth of the people. Therefore Moses expressly forbade the use of the female. Yet lest anyone, since only the female was forbidden, should imagine that eating the male was permitted to him, I shall now endeavour to prove something hitherto unknown: namely, that Moses, after beginning with the female as the better known, forbade the male as well, and that he is signified by the word תחמס thachmas, which follows immediately. And so these words of Moses, You shall not eat, etc., את בת היענה ואת התחמס, the daughter of jaana and the thachmas, are to be translated thus: You shall not eat the female ostrich, nor the male ostrich. To this pertains the following chapter, in which it is proved that the word תחמס thachmas, hitherto unknown, signifies the male ostrich.
